Getting started with daos

Source: vignettes/daos.Rmd
daos.Rmd

The daos package is a collection of utility functions built for day-to-day statistical work. This vignette walks through every function with short, self-contained examples.

Five bodies of work that started here have since grown into packages of their own, and are not covered below: taskr for task management, statbank for the Greenland and Faroese statbanks, cvrr for published Danish annual reports, taxmill for milling PDF financial statements into data, and pathr for the file browser and the RStudio addins that take the friction out of Windows paths. None of them depends on daos, or daos on them.

Convenience shorthands

f(): string interpolation

f() is a short alias for glue::glue(), inspired by Python’s f-string syntax. The name is not self-explanatory, but it is fast to type and stays out of the way in a pipeline.

year <- 2026
f("Report for {year}")
#> Report for 2026
f("1 + 1 = {1 + 1}")
#> 1 + 1 = 2

nowf(): formatted timestamp

nowf() combines format() and Sys.time() in a single call, so you can timestamp an export inline without stopping to look up the format(Sys.time(), ...) signature.

nowf()                  # default: YYYYMMDD
#> [1] "20261028"
nowf("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M")  # custom format
#> [1] "2026-10-28 09:15"

A typical use is timestamping an export file:

iris |>
  writexl::write_xlsx(f("iris_{nowf('%Y%B')}.xlsx"))

shh(): suppress messages and warnings

A shorthand for suppressMessages(suppressWarnings(...)). Useful when you are tired of tidyverse startup banners, or when an R script runs as a CLI tool (e.g. with rapp) or in a presentation tool like presenterm, where console output has to be clean. The odd name is on purpose: a function called quiet is one masking conflict away from trouble.

shh(message("this will not appear"))
shh(warning("neither will this"))

is_blank(): comprehensive blank test

is.na() only catches NA, and rlang::is_empty() only catches NULL and zero-length vectors. is_blank() covers all three plus empty strings, which is handy when validating input that can arrive in any of these forms.

is_blank(NULL)        # TRUE
#> [1] TRUE
is_blank(NA)          # TRUE
#> [1] TRUE
is_blank("")          # TRUE
#> [1] TRUE
is_blank(c(NA, NA))   # TRUE
#> [1] TRUE
is_blank(0)           # FALSE
#> [1] FALSE
is_blank("text")      # FALSE
#> [1] FALSE

%??%: null-coalescing with blank detection

Like rlang::%||% but uses is_blank() instead of is.null(), so it also triggers on NA, "", and empty vectors.

NULL %??% "default"
#> [1] "default"
NA   %??% 0
#> [1] 0
""   %??% "unknown"
#> [1] "unknown"
42   %??% 99          # returns 42
#> [1] 42

%like%: regex matching with NA preservation

%like% is a more readable replacement for str_detect(). The infix form reads naturally in a filter() call, and unlike grepl(), NA values stay NA instead of being coerced to FALSE. That matters when filtering on optional fields.

c("sedan", "SUV", NA, "truck") %like% "^S"
#> [1] FALSE  TRUE    NA FALSE

# In a dplyr pipeline:
filter(ggplot2::mpg, model %like% "\\d+") |>
  count(model)
#> # A tibble: 19 × 2
#>    model                      n
#>    <chr>                  <int>
#>  1 4runner 4wd                6
#>  2 a4                         7
#>  3 a4 quattro                 8
#>  4 a6 quattro                 3
#>  5 c1500 suburban 2wd         5
#>  6 caravan 2wd               11
#>  7 dakota pickup 4wd          9
#>  8 durango 4wd                7
#>  9 expedition 2wd             3
#> 10 explorer 4wd               6
#> 11 f150 pickup 4wd            7
#> 12 grand cherokee 4wd         8
#> 13 k1500 tahoe 4wd            4
#> 14 land cruiser wagon 4wd     2
#> 15 mountaineer 4wd            4
#> 16 navigator 2wd              3
#> 17 pathfinder 4wd             4
#> 18 ram 1500 pickup 4wd       10
#> 19 toyota tacoma 4wd          7

Files: the lazer package

The readers and writers have moved to their own package, lazer: read_files(), read_workbook(), inspect_excel(), write_excel(), read_access() and read_sut(), write_sut() and convert_sut() for supply and use table files (SUT, the TA files). Use library(lazer), and see vignette("lazer", package = "lazer").

summon(): retrieve objects by name pattern

A regex-based alternative to ls() + mget():

mget(ls(pattern = "dat\\d"))   # base R
summon("dat\\d")               # daos

summon() pairs naturally with out = "unpack" to collect a family of objects back into a list:

dat1 <- data.frame(x = 1)
dat2 <- data.frame(x = 2)
dat3 <- data.frame(x = 3)

result <- summon("^dat\\d+$")
names(result)
#> [1] "dat1" "dat2" "dat3"

Data inspection

view_types(): compare column types across data frames

view_types() is glimpse() across several data frames at once: one row per column, with the type in each dataset. Useful before a join, or before binding with read_files(out = "bind").

The status column says whether the frames would bind: ok, coercible (types differ but combine, like int + dbl or an all-NA column with anything), missing (absent somewhere, which bind_rows() fills with NA), or conflict (the bind fails).

df_a <- data.frame(x = 1L,  y = "a", z = NA)
df_b <- data.frame(x = 1.0, y = 2,   z = "b", w = 1)

view_types(df_a, df_b)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   column status    df_a  df_b 
#>   <chr>  <chr>     <chr> <chr>
#> 1 x      coercible int   dbl  
#> 2 y      conflict  chr   dbl  
#> 3 z      coercible lgl   chr  
#> 4 w      missing   NA    dbl
# Only the columns that would break a bind:
view_types(df_a, df_b, diff = TRUE)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   column status   df_a  df_b 
#>   <chr>  <chr>    <chr> <chr>
#> 1 y      conflict chr   dbl

The output of read_files() can be passed directly, since a named list of data frames is unpacked:

lazer::read_files("data/dat{2020:2023}.parquet", names = 2020:2023) |>
  view_types(diff = TRUE)

The focus argument checks that specific columns have an expected type and returns only the datasets where they do not:

view_types(df_a, df_b, focus = c(x = "int", y = "chr"))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>   column status    df_b 
#>   <chr>  <chr>     <chr>
#> 1 x      coercible dbl  
#> 2 y      conflict  dbl

flag_duplicates(): detect and label duplicate rows

Base R’s duplicated() only marks the second occurrence of a duplicate. flag_duplicates() marks all copies and gives them a shared group ID, so the whole group can be inspected together. The ID can also serve as an implicit record linkage key: if several respondents have reported the same information but background data is missing for one of them, the shared dupid reveals the connection.

flag_duplicates(ggplot2::mpg)
#> # A tibble: 234 × 13
#>    isdup dupid manufacturer model      displ  year   cyl trans drv     cty   hwy
#>    <lgl> <int> <chr>        <chr>      <dbl> <int> <int> <chr> <chr> <int> <int>
#>  1 FALSE     0 audi         a4           1.8  1999     4 auto… f        18    29
#>  2 FALSE     0 audi         a4           1.8  1999     4 manu… f        21    29
#>  3 FALSE     0 audi         a4           2    2008     4 manu… f        20    31
#>  4 FALSE     0 audi         a4           2    2008     4 auto… f        21    30
#>  5 FALSE     0 audi         a4           2.8  1999     6 auto… f        16    26
#>  6 FALSE     0 audi         a4           2.8  1999     6 manu… f        18    26
#>  7 FALSE     0 audi         a4           3.1  2008     6 auto… f        18    27
#>  8 FALSE     0 audi         a4 quattro   1.8  1999     4 manu… 4        18    26
#>  9 FALSE     0 audi         a4 quattro   1.8  1999     4 auto… 4        16    25
#> 10 FALSE     0 audi         a4 quattro   2    2008     4 manu… 4        20    28
#> # ℹ 224 more rows
#> # ℹ 2 more variables: fl <chr>, class <chr>
# Check specific columns:
flag_duplicates(ggplot2::mpg, manufacturer, model, year) |>
  filter(isdup) |>
  arrange(dupid)
#> # A tibble: 227 × 13
#>    isdup dupid manufacturer model      displ  year   cyl trans drv     cty   hwy
#>    <lgl> <int> <chr>        <chr>      <dbl> <int> <int> <chr> <chr> <int> <int>
#>  1 TRUE      1 audi         a4           1.8  1999     4 auto… f        18    29
#>  2 TRUE      1 audi         a4           1.8  1999     4 manu… f        21    29
#>  3 TRUE      1 audi         a4           2.8  1999     6 auto… f        16    26
#>  4 TRUE      1 audi         a4           2.8  1999     6 manu… f        18    26
#>  5 TRUE      2 audi         a4           2    2008     4 manu… f        20    31
#>  6 TRUE      2 audi         a4           2    2008     4 auto… f        21    30
#>  7 TRUE      2 audi         a4           3.1  2008     6 auto… f        18    27
#>  8 TRUE      3 audi         a4 quattro   1.8  1999     4 manu… 4        18    26
#>  9 TRUE      3 audi         a4 quattro   1.8  1999     4 auto… 4        16    25
#> 10 TRUE      3 audi         a4 quattro   2.8  1999     6 auto… 4        15    25
#> # ℹ 217 more rows
#> # ℹ 2 more variables: fl <chr>, class <chr>

Both functions inspect data before you settle on a rule. Turning a rule into a checkpoint is the job of the expectr package, below.

Data validation: the expectr package

The validation checkpoints, expect_empty(), expect_none(), expect_unique(), expect_balanced(), expect_no_overlap() and tally_violations(), have moved to their own package, expectr. They share an engine and a contract the rest of daos does not: each states an expectation about data as “the set of violations must be empty”.

Load expectr to use them:

library(expectr)

lazer::read_files("data/dat{2020:2023}.parquet", names = 2020:2023) |>
  view_types(diff = TRUE) |>
  expect_empty(warn_msg = "The files do not bind")

See vignette("expectr", package = "expectr").

Data manipulation

drop_empty_rows() and drop_empty_cols(): selective removal

Choose which columns determine whether a row is empty, so an ID or metadata column does not keep an otherwise empty observation. Selection works like select(): names, ranges, starts_with(), where(is.numeric), and all_of(). With no selection, every column is inspected.

df <- tibble::tibble(
  id = 1:3,
  score_a = c(1, NA, NA),
  score_b = c(NA_real_, NA_real_, NA_real_),
  comment = c("ok", "", "  ")
)

# Inspect the score columns; keep every column in retained rows.
drop_empty_rows(df, starts_with("score_"))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>      id score_a score_b comment
#>   <int>   <dbl>   <dbl> <chr>  
#> 1     1       1      NA ok

# Only numeric columns are candidates for removal; id is not empty.
drop_empty_cols(df, where(is.numeric))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>      id score_a comment
#>   <int>   <dbl> <chr>  
#> 1     1       1 "ok"   
#> 2     2      NA ""     
#> 3     3      NA "  "

# Include empty and whitespace-only text, without modifying retained values.
drop_empty_rows(df, comment, blank = TRUE)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>      id score_a score_b comment
#>   <int>   <dbl>   <dbl> <chr>  
#> 1     1       1      NA ok

# Combine row and column removal explicitly.
df |> drop_empty_rows(starts_with("score_")) |> drop_empty_cols()
#> # A tibble: 1 × 3
#>      id score_a comment
#>   <int>   <dbl> <chr>  
#> 1     1       1 ok

By default, only missing values (NA and NaN) count as empty. blank = TRUE also handles blank character values and factor labels. Zero and FALSE always count as data. A row is removed only when all selected values are empty. Column removal only affects the selected columns.

An empty selection changes nothing. Zero-row inputs retain their column schema; zero-column inputs retain their rows. Grouped data is assessed over the whole input, and grouping metadata is updated when columns are removed.

split_by(): split a data frame into a named list

dplyr::group_split() returns an unnamed list. split_by() adds names derived from the grouping values, making it straightforward to index by group:

parts <- split_by(ggplot2::mpg, manufacturer)
names(parts)[1:5]
#> [1] "audi"      "chevrolet" "dodge"     "ford"      "honda"
head(parts[["audi"]])
#> # A tibble: 6 × 11
#>   manufacturer model displ  year   cyl trans      drv     cty   hwy fl    class 
#>   <chr>        <chr> <dbl> <int> <int> <chr>      <chr> <int> <int> <chr> <chr> 
#> 1 audi         a4      1.8  1999     4 auto(l5)   f        18    29 p     compa…
#> 2 audi         a4      1.8  1999     4 manual(m5) f        21    29 p     compa…
#> 3 audi         a4      2    2008     4 manual(m6) f        20    31 p     compa…
#> 4 audi         a4      2    2008     4 auto(av)   f        21    30 p     compa…
#> 5 audi         a4      2.8  1999     6 auto(l5)   f        16    26 p     compa…
#> 6 audi         a4      2.8  1999     6 manual(m5) f        18    26 p     compa…

Multiple grouping columns are joined with .sep:

parts2 <- split_by(ggplot2::mpg, cyl, drv, .sep = "-")
names(parts2)[1:4]
#> [1] "4-4" "4-f" "5-f" "6-4"

spells_to_panel(): from spells to a yearly panel

Registers often store spells: one row per education, address or benefit period, with a start, an end and a status. spells_to_panel() turns them into one row per unit and year (or by = "quarter"/"month"), with the status at primo and ultimo. By default primo is the previous ultimo, so primo 2021 is the status on 31 December 2020.

In an education register the status is the outcome of the spell, passed or dropped out. With status_is = "outcome", a running spell shows as ongoing and the outcome applies from the end date until a new spell starts:

education <- data.frame(
  cpr    = c("a", "a", "b"),
  start  = as.Date(c("2018-08-15", "2021-08-15", "2019-08-15")),
  end    = as.Date(c("2021-06-20", NA,           "2020-03-01")),
  status = c("passed", "in progress", "dropped out")
)

education |>
  spells_to_panel(cpr, start, end, status,
                  from = 2018, to = 2022,
                  status_is = "outcome", ongoing = "in progress")
#> # A tibble: 10 × 4
#>    cpr    year primo       ultimo     
#>    <chr> <int> <chr>       <chr>      
#>  1 a      2018 NA          in progress
#>  2 a      2019 in progress in progress
#>  3 a      2020 in progress in progress
#>  4 a      2021 in progress in progress
#>  5 a      2022 in progress in progress
#>  6 b      2018 NA          NA         
#>  7 b      2019 NA          in progress
#>  8 b      2020 in progress dropped out
#>  9 b      2021 dropped out dropped out
#> 10 b      2022 dropped out dropped out

With the default status_is = "state", the status holds for the whole spell (enrolled, on leave) and is NA outside spells. from and to give every unit the same window, which makes a balanced panel. Without them, each unit runs from its first start to its last end. Dates are handled as integer days, and one compiled pass over the sorted spells does the work, so millions of spells take seconds.

add_spell_status(): status from spells on a panel you already have

Often the panel exists already, e.g. a population with one row per person and year, and the spells should only add a status to it. A left_join(join_by(between())) does that until the data gets messy: overlapping spells duplicate rows, and an ongoing spell with no end matches nothing. add_spell_status() keeps the rows of the panel exactly as they are and uses the rules of spells_to_panel():

population <- data.frame(cpr  = c("a", "a", "b", "c"),
                         year = c(2020, 2021, 2020, 2020))

population |>
  add_spell_status(education, cpr, year, start, end, status,
                   status_is = "outcome", ongoing = "in progress")
#>   cpr year status_primo status_ultimo
#> 1   a 2020  in progress   in progress
#> 2   a 2021  in progress   in progress
#> 3   b 2020  in progress   dropped out
#> 4   c 2020         <NA>          <NA>

A Date column in at gives the status on that day instead, e.g. the day of a diagnosis. Use when = "ultimo" for a single column, name to choose its name, and overlap = "error" to stop when spells overlap.

Domain-specific

clean_cpr() / clean_cvr(): standardise identifier columns

Identifiers rarely arrive in one consistent shape: 111111-1118, 12 34 56 78, DK12345678, or a nine-digit CPR that lost its leading zero in Excel. Before a join, both sides need the same form, and that is all these two functions do. They take a vector and return a vector, so the natural place for them is inside a mutate():

clean_cpr(c("111111-1118", "101004007", "1111111118"))
#> [1] "1111111118" "0101004007" "1111111118"
clean_cvr(c("DK12345678", "12 34 56 78", "12345678"))
#> [1] "12345678" "12345678" "12345678"

The two differ on one point. clean_cpr() zero-pads nine-digit values, because birth days 01 to 09 mean that a third of all CPR numbers start with a zero, which Excel drops. clean_cvr() never adds a digit: a seven-digit CVR cannot be told apart from a typo, and padding it would let a malformed number slip past a later cvr %like% "^\\d{8}$" checkpoint.

Neither function validates. Malformed values come back cleaned but still visibly malformed. Validation is add_cpr_info()’s job (below), or a checkpoint from expectr.

format_db07(): choose the format of DB07 industry codes

DB07 industry codes appear both as 011100 and 01.11.00 depending on the source. format_db07() automatically handles mixed input with dots, whitespace, or digits only. Choose "dotted" (the default) or "compact" output without specifying the input format. Any aggregation level works:

format_db07(c("011100", "01.1100", "0111", "011"))
#> [1] "01.11.00" "01.11.00" "01.11"    "01.1"
format_db07(c("011100", "01.11.00", "01 11 00"), format = "compact")
#> [1] "011100" "011100" "011100"

Like the clean_* functions, format_db07() never invents digits: a code that lost its leading zero in Excel is ambiguous (111 could be group 11.1 or class 01.11), so keep industry codes as character columns.

db_label(): add Danish industry labels

Use db_label() to add a label column from a DB code. Always specify version = "DB07" or version = "DB25"; identical codes can have different meanings in the two classifications.

df <- data.frame(dbkode = c("011200", "01.49.10", NA))
df |> dplyr::mutate(branche_label = db_label(dbkode, version = "DB07"))
#>     dbkode   branche_label
#> 1   011200 Dyrkning af ris
#> 2 01.49.10        Kenneler
#> 3     <NA>            <NA>
db_label(c("A", "01", "01.1", "01.11"), version = "DB25")
#> [1] "LANDBRUG, JAGT, SKOVBRUG OG FISKERI"                              
#> [2] "Plante- og husdyravl, jagt og serviceydelser i forbindelse hermed"
#> [3] "Dyrkning af etårige afgrøder"                                     
#> [4] "Dyrkning af korn (undtagen ris), bælgfrugter og olieholdige frø"

Labels come from the bundled DST tables and work offline. Input can contain dots or whitespace. Unknown codes return NA with a warning; missing values stay missing. Keep leading zeroes in character codes.

Convert industry codes between DB07 and DB25

For mixed data, inspect the source codes before converting:

inspect_db(c("014910", "014800", "253000", "011200", NA))
#> # A tibble: 5 × 5
#>   input  code   status    label_db07                                  label_db25
#>   <chr>  <chr>  <chr>     <chr>                                       <chr>     
#> 1 014910 014910 db07_only Kenneler                                    NA        
#> 2 014800 014800 db25_only NA                                          Avl af an…
#> 3 253000 253000 both      Fremstilling af dampkedler undtagen centra… Fremstill…
#> 4 011200 011200 both      Dyrkning af ris                             Dyrkning …
#> 5 NA     NA     missing   NA                                          NA

db07_only and db25_only indicate membership in just one classification. both means the version cannot be determined from the code alone: 253000 has different meanings in DB07 and DB25. Both labels are returned for review. Identical labels also leave the version unresolved. Use source metadata and the original industry text and time context to investigate these rows. The inspection supports full six-digit codes only.

convert_db07_to_db25() and convert_db25_to_db07() use bundled keys from Statistics Denmark (source page updated 26 February 2026), so no internet connection is needed. Both accept full six-digit codes with or without dots and whitespace:

convert_db07_to_db25(c("011100", "01.49.10", NA))
#> [1] "01.11.00" "01.48.00" NA
convert_db25_to_db07("25.30.00", format = "compact")
#> [1] "254000"

By default, a code with multiple possible destinations returns NA with a warning. To choose DST’s simplified mapping explicitly:

convert_db07_to_db25("01.19.00", method = "simple")
#> [1] "01.19.00"
convert_db25_to_db07("01.48.00", method = "simple")
#> [1] "01.49.10"

The simplified matrices are specific to each direction and use numbers of units, not economic activity. They are approximate and should not be used as weights to distribute turnover. A round trip need not recover the original code. Invalid lengths and unknown codes return NA with a warning; missing values remain missing. Leading zeroes are not guessed.

add_cpr_info(): add birth date, age, sex, and validity

add_cpr_info() appends selected information while preserving the original CPR column. Dashes, spaces, and lost leading zeroes are handled internally. Use clean_cpr() explicitly if you also want to standardise the source column.

Both functions share the same native cleaning rules. add_cpr_info() parses each CPR once for all requested outputs, including multiple age calculations. You do not need a separate cleaning step just to calculate CPR information. Use an explicit cleaning step when the identifier will also be used for joins or export:

df |>
  dplyr::mutate(pnr = clean_cpr(pnr)) |>
  add_cpr_info(pnr, age(year), sex, bday)

clean_cpr() is idempotent: cleaning again gives the same values. Already standardised character vectors are returned without a replacement vector.

Without selections, the function adds bday, age, sex, mod11, and valid. Bare age and age() use today’s date; explicit references make analysis reproducible.

df <- data.frame(
  pnr = c("1111111118", "111111-1118", "111111118"),
  year = c(2024L, 2025L, 2026L)
)
add_cpr_info(df, pnr)
#>           pnr year       bday age sex mod11 valid
#> 1  1111111118 2024 1911-11-11 114   0  TRUE  TRUE
#> 2 111111-1118 2025 1911-11-11 114   0  TRUE  TRUE
#> 3   111111118 2026 1911-11-01 114   0 FALSE  TRUE
add_cpr_info(df, pnr, sex, birth_date = bday)
#>           pnr year sex birth_date
#> 1  1111111118 2024   0 1911-11-11
#> 2 111111-1118 2025   0 1911-11-11
#> 3   111111118 2026   0 1911-11-01

Write output_name = calculation to rename a result. Each age calculation has its own reference, so several ages can be added in one call:

df |>
  add_cpr_info(
    pnr,
    primoalder = age(year),
    medioalder = age(year, "medio"),
    ultimoalder = age(year, "ultimo"),
    sex,
    bday
  )
#>           pnr year primoalder medioalder ultimoalder sex       bday
#> 1  1111111118 2024        112        112         113   0 1911-11-11
#> 2 111111-1118 2025        113        113         114   0 1911-11-11
#> 3   111111118 2026        114        114         115   0 1911-11-01

age(year) defaults to "primo" with primo = "previous_ultimo" (31 December of the previous year); "medio" means 1 July and "ultimo" means 31 December. year can be a scalar, a column, or an expression evaluated in the original input data.

This default makes opening ages equal to the previous year’s closing ages. It can also be written explicitly:

add_cpr_info(df, pnr, primoalder = age(year, primo = "previous_ultimo"))
#>           pnr year primoalder
#> 1  1111111118 2024        112
#> 2 111111-1118 2025        113
#> 3   111111118 2026        114

Someone born on 1 January 2000 is then 0 in counting year 2001; age(year, primo = "jan1") instead includes that day’s birthday and gives 1.

For a specific date, use age(date = ...) with a Date or ISO date string. Supply one reference for all rows or one per row. Missing references give missing ages. Use .env$name to explicitly access a caller variable when a column has the same name.

add_cpr_info(df, pnr, alder = age(date = "2025-07-01"))
#>           pnr year alder
#> 1  1111111118 2024   113
#> 2 111111-1118 2025   113
#> 3   111111118 2026   113
df$reference <- as.Date(paste0(df$year, "-01-01"))
add_cpr_info(df, pnr, alder = age(date = reference))
#>           pnr year  reference alder
#> 1  1111111118 2024 2024-01-01   112
#> 2 111111-1118 2025 2025-01-01   113
#> 3   111111118 2026 2026-01-01   114

Existing output names cause an error with guidance to rename the selection or use overwrite = TRUE. Duplicate output names are always an error, and the source CPR column cannot be overwritten.

valid means ten digits encoding a real calendar date, not confirmation that the CPR number was assigned. Missing and invalid CPR values give valid = FALSE. mod11 is an independent checksum and is not part of valid. Choose mod11 explicitly when selecting outputs if you need it.

The former add, ref_date, year, and at arguments are replaced by selections and age(). For example, add = c(alder = "age"), year = year becomes alder = age(year). The source CPR column is now preserved.

Age counts completed calendar years, not elapsed days divided by 365.25. For a person born on 29 February, age increases on 29 February in leap years and on 1 March in non-leap years. For a birth date of 29 February 2000:

Reference date Age
2024-02-28 23
2024-02-29 24
2024-03-01 24
2025-02-28 24
2025-03-01 25

age(2024) means age on 31 December 2023. by default, giving age 23 in this example.

Interactive tools

screen_timeseries(): interactive time-series screening

It is hard to get as close to data in a console as in Excel, where the feedback is immediate and visual. screen_timeseries() is an attempt to bridge that gap. It launches a Shiny app where you walk through the time series group by group, zoom, and flag anomalies – without writing any filtering code.

All columns that are not x, y, series, or excluded automatically become dropdown filters. Requires shiny and plotly. Group row indices are prepared once, and plots are built directly with Plotly for fast navigation.

df <- expand.grid(
  year    = 2010:2020,
  country = c("DK", "SE", "NO", "FI")
)
df$gdp <- rnorm(nrow(df), mean = 300, sd = 30)

screen_timeseries(df, x = year, y = gdp)

# Multiple lines per group with series:
ggplot2::economics_long |>
  mutate(group = "Economics") |>
  screen_timeseries(date, value, series = variable, .exclude = value01)

Keyboard shortcuts

Key Action
<- / -> Navigate to previous / next group
Space Flag the current group
R Reset zoom
Q Quit and return flagged groups

The .y_min and .y_max arguments fix the Y-axis bounds globally across all groups. The .title argument sets a title shown in the app header and in downloaded figures:

screen_timeseries(df, year, gdp,
                  .y_min = 0, .y_max = 500,
                  .title = "GDP by country")

Press Q, click Finish, or close the browser session to end screening. The function returns flagged group keys invisibly and also prints pasteable R code such as flagged <- tibble::tibble(country = c("DK", "NO")). This preserves the result even if you did not assign the call to an object. Use .print = FALSE to suppress the console code when desired. Reloading the browser also ends its session, so restart screen_timeseries() to begin again.

Choose diagnostics inside the app

All diagnostic tools start switched off. Select any combination of Statistics, Seasonality, Outliers, Stationarity, Autocorrelation, and Structural breaks using the checkboxes. Only selected tools run; results are cached within the session. Your choices remain active as you navigate through groups. With multiple lines, use Series to diagnose to choose one line for analysis.

Results share a compact panel inside the main graph card. Switch between enabled analyses using the tabs; each shows its conclusion alongside the figures or a small diagnostic plot. Overview gathers the main findings; click a finding to open that analysis. Data quality, full outlier tables and method notes open in dialogs. On desktop screens, the graph adjusts its height to keep the active results in view. Keys 1 to 6 toggle tools in sidebar order; arrow keys on a focused result tab switch tabs.

  • Seasonality adds a dashed trend-plus-season line to the main plot and a seasonal profile alongside it. The profile is in the original units.
  • Outliers marks unusual residual observations on the main plot.
  • Autocorrelation displays ACF and PACF plots below the main plot.
  • Stationarity shows KPSS and Phillips–Perron results, including their different null hypotheses and interpretations.
  • Structural breaks marks candidate dates on the main plot and displays confidence limits. Choose a level or trend model in the app.

The Seasonal period control sets observations per seasonal cycle, such as 12 for monthly observations with annual seasonality. Leave it blank to infer annual seasonality for calendar months/quarters; other indices default to 1 (no seasonality). .period = 12 can pre-fill this control, but does not enable any tool. Gaps, duplicate dates and missing/non-finite values are reported, and prevent time-dependent analysis without silently modifying data.

Descriptive statistics, decomposition, outlier screening and correlations use base R. Stationarity tests additionally need feasts and urca; structural breaks need strucchange. The app explains unavailable analyses. Break searches are limited to 30–2000 observations, use BIC to choose up to three breaks, and require segments of at least 15% (and at least 10 observations). Outlier and break markers are candidates for review, not corrections.

The same diagnostic engine is available outside Shiny. Group explicitly by the columns identifying one time series:

df |>
  group_by(country) |>
  diagnose_timeseries(year, gdp, .features = c("summary", "stationarity"))

This returns one row per group with scalar statistics and list columns for test results, outliers, break dates, correlations, decomposition and notes. See ?diagnose_timeseries for sample-size requirements and method details.
